question: The headline says D-PLEX100 reduced surgical-site infections by 60%, and SHIELD II enrolled 975 patients. Is it accurate to present that as the primary-endpoint benefit for every patient undergoing abdominal surgery? Explain exactly which claims the available evidence supports.

answer.answer:
No. That presentation conflates the endpoint, analysis population and scope of applicability. PolyPid’s 60% relative reduction matches the secondary, SSI-only result in 768 evaluable participants—not the primary endpoint or all 975 randomized participants. The primary endpoint combined incisional SSI, re-intervention and death; it showed approximately a 40% relative reduction in the 798-participant, >20 cm incision population. Both comparisons tested D-PLEX plus standard of care against standard of care alone. [polypid-q2; trial-shield2]

Accurate wording: “Sponsor-reported SHIELD II results showed improved 30-day composite outcomes and fewer incisional SSIs with adjunctive D-PLEX in the specified colorectal-surgery analysis populations.” These are group-level findings, not evidence of a 60% primary-endpoint benefit for every abdominal-surgery patient. [trial-shield2]

claims.claim: Reporting and comparison: PolyPid is both the press-release issuer and the responsible sponsor for the ClinicalTrials.gov record. SHIELD II was a randomized, controlled, blinded Phase 3 trial comparing locally administered D-PLEX plus prophylactic standard of care with standard of care alone. The registry reports 975 randomized participants: 487 versus 488. These are sponsor-reported results, not an independent FDA efficacy determination.

Primary endpoint: In the registry-labeled intent-to-treat population with target incision length >20 cm, 405 D-PLEX-plus-SoC and 393 SoC participants were analyzed. Treatment failure meant at least one adjudicated target-incision SSI, target-incision re-intervention, or death from any cause within 30 days. Rates were 10.9% versus 18.1%; reported risk difference −7.2 percentage points (95% CI −12.1 to −2.3), p=0.0039. Approximately 40% relative reduction is calculated from the displayed rates—not 60%. This composite result does not independently establish reductions in every component.

The 60% headline: The secondary endpoint measured at least one adjudicated superficial and/or deep incisional SSI at the target incision by day 30. It used evaluable participants with non-missing outcomes from the ITT population: 391 versus 377, totaling 768. Rates were 3.8% versus 9.5%, p=0.0013; 1−3.8/9.5=60%, consistent with PolyPid’s headline. The registry reports a risk difference of −5.8 percentage points (95% CI −9.3 to −2.3). Thus the absolute benefit was about six percentage points, not 60 percentage points; this is neither an all-randomized SSI analysis nor a guaranteed individual benefit.

What the full 975 support: A separate secondary 30-day composite endpoint, titled for target incision length >7 cm and labeled 'All randomized population,' analyzed 487 versus 488 participants. Rates were 11.1% versus 17.4%, p=0.0047—a calculated 6.3-percentage-point difference. This supports a favorable composite comparison in that trial population, not a 60% SSI-only primary-endpoint result.

Additional secondary evidence: The posted ASEPSIS >20 wound-assessment endpoint showed 2.0% versus 5.6% in 391 versus 377 evaluable participants, p=0.0103. The posted endpoint results are directionally consistent with PolyPid’s statement that the primary and key secondary endpoints were met, subject to the analysis-plan limitations below.

Applicability is restricted: The registry describes adults undergoing elective colorectal resection, with or without a stoma; its current eligibility text requires a target incision >20 cm and preoperative hemodynamic stability. Exclusions include suspected perforation, intra-abdominal abscess, specified urgent/emergency obstruction cases, active infection and other medical restrictions. Participants were predominantly White (973/975), with only four enrolled in the United States. These facts limit direct generalization; they do not prove lack of benefit elsewhere. Benefit for every abdominal procedure, excluded patient group, demographic subgroup or individual is not established.

Regulatory scope: PolyPid describes its NDA as seeking SSI prevention in abdominal colorectal surgery. Its August update reports FDA acceptance with Priority Review on July 27, 2026, and a November 28, 2026 PDUFA goal date. As of the question’s date, these supplied documents establish a company-reported review milestone—not approval, a final label, or authorization for all abdominal surgery.

uncertainties: The registry lists protocol and statistical-analysis-plan files, but their contents are not supplied. The snapshot does not fully reconcile current >20 cm eligibility wording with the >7 cm all-randomized analysis or establish the amendment history, prespecification, multiplicity controls and complete analysis-set rules. [trial-shield2]

The SSI-only analysis excludes 30 participants from the registry-labeled ITT denominator because it uses non-missing outcome data. The supplied results do not establish how alternative missing-data assumptions would affect that estimate. [trial-shield2]

The all-randomized composite analysis labels its −6.3 estimate and negative confidence limits as a 'Risk Ratio.' That is internally inconsistent with a risk ratio; the displayed rates imply a 6.3-percentage-point difference, but the reporting label requires clarification. [trial-shield2]

No FDA review assessment or approved labeling is supplied. Neither statistically favorable trial results nor Priority Review and a target date establish the eventual regulatory outcome or label breadth. [polypid-q2]
